notes:
Task and constraints: Find the shortest contiguous subarray whose degree equals the degree of the full array.
Idea: Count frequencies and record the first and last index of each value, then minimize spans among values with maximum frequency.
Technique and why it applies: A value's degree is its count. Its shortest subarray containing all occurrences extends from its first occurrence to its last; the maximum count determines which values qualify.
Invariant: left and right store the earliest and latest indices for each number seen, while counts gives the array degree.
Edge cases: A single distinct value produces the full array length. Empty input would make max(counts.values()) fail, though the problem gives a nonempty array.
Complexity: One pass builds counts and boundaries, then a scan checks candidates, giving O(n) expected time and O(u) space for u distinct values. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether nums can be partitioned into k subsets with equal sums.
Idea: Backtrack through sorted or input-order elements, filling one subset to the target sum before starting the next.
Technique and why it applies: visited prevents reusing elements; curr accumulates the current subset. Reaching limit recurses to the next subset, while duplicate-value skipping and empty-subset pruning reduce branches.
Invariant: visited marks numbers assigned to completed or current subsets, and cnt counts subsets already completed.
Edge cases: The total must divide evenly by k, and no number may exceed target. The code returns False when len(nums)<k, which is valid only if each subset must be nonempty.
Complexity: Backtracking is exponential in n in the worst case, with O(n) visited state and recursion. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether the numbers can be divided into k equal-sum subsets.
Idea: Sort numbers descending and backtrack by assigning each number to one of k subset totals.
Technique and why it applies: A candidate is skipped if adding it exceeds target. On failure, the sum is restored; if a bucket remains empty after backtracking, trying equivalent empty buckets is redundant and the loop breaks.
Invariant: subset_sums stores the current total of each bucket, and each recursion level assigns one additional number.
Edge cases: If total is not divisible by k or the largest value exceeds target, return False. The method sorts nums in place.
Complexity: Worst-case search is exponential; the author O(k^(n-k)·k!) is a broad bound. Auxiliary space is O(n) for recursion and bucket sums, matching the space label.

Task and constraints: Decide whether nums can be partitioned into k equal-sum subsets.
Idea: Memoize subset choices with a bitmask of used indices and track the remaining total to fill.
Technique and why it applies: The next subset's target remainder is derived from todo modulo target. For each unused value no larger than that remainder, the recursion marks its bit and checks whether the rest can be partitioned.
Invariant: lookup[used] caches whether the subset of indices represented by used can complete a valid partition.
Edge cases: Divisibility and maximum-element checks reject impossible cases. lookup[-1] is set True for the all-used mask; the empty mask starts the recursion.
Complexity: There are O(2^n) masks and up to O(n) candidates per state, giving O(n·2^n) time and O(2^n) memo space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum height after each square is dropped onto a line, where it stacks on any overlapping squares.
Idea: Compress square endpoints and use square-root decomposition with per-position heights and block maximums.
Technique and why it applies: Each square's interval is queried for its highest current surface, then its side length is added. Partial blocks are scanned individually while complete blocks use summary arrays; max_height tracks the global skyline height.
Invariant: heights stores individual compressed-coordinate values, blocks and blocks_read summarize block maxima for range query/update operations.
Edge cases: The code contains SegmentTree classes that are not used by fallingSquares. Endpoint compression and bisect rely on index positions representing intervals; the sqrt block size can be zero for tiny coordinate sets unless at least one block is guaranteed.
Complexity: The active query/update loops are intended O(sqrt(n)) per square, giving O(n·sqrt(n)) time and O(n) space, consistent with labels.

Task and constraints: Compute the maximum stacked height after each square lands on all earlier overlapping squares.
Idea: For each square, scan later squares and propagate its height to those whose horizontal intervals overlap, then take prefix maxima.
Technique and why it applies: If square j overlaps square i, its base must be at least the height reached by i, so heights[j] is raised to heights[i]. The final pass converts each square's individual height into the running maximum height seen so far.
Invariant: heights[i] is the candidate top height of square i after contributions from earlier squares, and result stores the global maximum after each drop.
Edge cases: The condition uses half-open intervals [left,left+size), so touching edges do not overlap. The segment tree classes defined above are unused by this solution.
Complexity: The nested loop is O(n²) time and the heights/result arrays use O(n) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum visible stack height after each square drop.
Idea: Compress square boundaries into sorted coordinates and maintain height values over the compressed intervals.
Technique and why it applies: bisect finds the covered coordinate range; the maximum existing height in that range determines the new square's top. The code replaces the affected coordinate slices with the new height and restores the neighboring boundary height.
Invariant: pos stores sorted compressed boundaries, heights stores surface levels at those boundaries, and maxH is the maximum top height so far.
Edge cases: The implementation assumes compressed boundaries are maintained in a consistent paired order. It uses list slicing and max over a range rather than the declared segment-tree classes; these operations may shift many entries.
Complexity: Slice updates can take O(n) per square, so overall time is O(n²) in the worst case and space O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find target in an ascending sorted array and return its index, or -1 if absent.
Idea: Apply binary search by repeatedly checking the middle element and discarding half the remaining interval.
Technique and why it applies: If nums[mid] is greater than target, all indices at mid and to its right can be excluded; if smaller, the left half can be excluded. Equality returns the index immediately.
Invariant: If target exists, its index remains within the inclusive interval [left,right].
Edge cases: Empty input initializes right to -1 and skips the loop, returning -1. Duplicate values may return any matching index, as permitted by the problem.
Complexity: The search halves the interval each iteration, giving O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Search for target in a sorted integer array.
Idea: Use an inclusive binary-search interval and update its bounds based on the midpoint comparison.
Technique and why it applies: The midpoint is calculated as left+(right-left)//2. If the midpoint value is too large or too small, the interval shrinks to the appropriate half; a match returns mid.
Invariant: The remaining interval contains every possible target position not yet ruled out.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return -1. The inclusive loop condition left<=right ensures the final single-element interval is checked.
Complexity: Each iteration halves the search interval, so time is O(log n) and extra space O(1), matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Convert uppercase English letters in str to lowercase while preserving all other characters.
Idea: Map each uppercase letter to its lowercase code using the offset between 'A' and 'a', then join the results.
Technique and why it applies: For characters in 'A' through 'Z', ord('a')+ord(c)-ord('A') computes the corresponding lowercase code point. Other characters are returned unchanged.
Invariant: The output list comprehension emits exactly one transformed character for each input character.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty string. The range test restricts conversion to ASCII uppercase letters, avoiding changes to punctuation and lowercase characters.
Complexity: The string is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(n) output storage. The author O(1) space label omits output construction.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum sum of ASCII values deleted from two strings to make them equal.
Idea: Memoize a recursive DP over prefix endpoints, choosing whether to delete a character from either string when endpoints differ.
Technique and why it applies: Matching characters require no deletion and recurse diagonally. Otherwise, the code adds the ASCII value of one endpoint to the cheaper subproblem. Base cases sum the remaining prefix when the other string is exhausted.
Invariant: fun(i,j) is the minimum delete cost to make s1[:i+1] and s2[:j+1] equal.
Edge cases: Empty prefixes are handled by summing remaining characters. The memo check occurs before base cases but only cached non-base states are stored. Repeated sum construction adds extra work.
Complexity: There are O(mn) states, but base cases sum slices repeatedly and may add O(m+n) per boundary call. Time is O(mn+m²+n²) in a loose bound, and memo space is O(mn). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum total ASCII deletion cost to make s1 and s2 equal.
Idea: Fill a full two-dimensional DP table for all prefixes of both strings.
Technique and why it applies: The first row and column accumulate the cost of deleting an entire prefix. Matching characters reuse the diagonal cost; mismatches choose the cheaper of deleting the current character from either string.
Invariant: dp[i][j] stores the minimum deletion cost for the first i characters of s1 and first j characters of s2.
Edge cases: Empty strings are handled by initialized first row and column. Equal characters are retained without deletion.
Complexity: The table has O(mn) cells with constant work per cell, so time and space are O(mn), matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum ASCII sum of characters deleted to make two strings identical.
Idea: Use two rolling DP rows instead of storing the full prefix table.
Technique and why it applies: Each cell depends only on the prior row, the current row's previous column, or the prior diagonal. Equal characters reuse the diagonal value; unequal characters add the cost of deleting one endpoint.
Invariant: dp[i%2][j] stores the minimum cost for the processed prefix of s1 and the first j characters of s2.
Edge cases: The first row is initialized by deleting prefixes of s2, and each new row initializes column zero by deleting the s1 prefix. Empty strings therefore work.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(mn) time and two rows use O(n) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Count contiguous subarrays whose product is strictly less than k, assuming positive integers.
Idea: Maintain a sliding window product and shrink its left boundary until the product falls below k.
Technique and why it applies: For each right endpoint, every subarray ending there and starting from left through right is valid, so fin-ini+1 is added to the count.
Invariant: p is the product of the current window nums[ini:fin+1], and all counted starts produce product below k.
Edge cases: k<=1 returns zero, which is correct for positive numbers. The inner loop assumes nums values are positive and can divide the product exactly when removing a value.
Complexity: Each pointer advances at most n times, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize stock trading profit with unlimited transactions and a fee charged on each sale.
Idea: Memoize a recursive state by day and whether the next action is to buy or sell.
Technique and why it applies: In buy state, choose purchasing today or skipping; in holding state, choose selling today with the fee deducted or keeping the stock. The recursion ends with zero profit after the final day.
Invariant: f(ind,buy) is the maximum future profit from day ind given the holding/buying state.
Edge cases: Empty prices returns zero through the base case, since ind==n immediately. The method allows no transaction and therefore never requires a negative final profit.
Complexity: There are O(n) memo states with constant work each, so time and space are O(n), plus O(n) recursion depth. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute maximum stock profit when each sale incurs a fixed transaction fee.
Idea: Track the best profit when holding no stock (cash) and when holding one share (hold).
Technique and why it applies: For each price, cash can stay unchanged or sell the held share after paying the fee; hold can stay unchanged or buy at today's price using previous cash. These states summarize all relevant transaction histories.
Invariant: cash is the best profit without a share after the processed day, and hold is the best net profit while holding one.
Edge cases: The code initializes hold=-prices[0], so it assumes prices is nonempty. It updates cash before hold, using the newly updated cash for buying; standard implementations often use old cash, so the in-place order should be checked for correctness.
Complexity: The loop is O(n) time and O(1) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the final character in a bit encoding is a one-bit character, given encodings 0 and 10/11.
Idea: Scan backward from the penultimate bit, toggling a parity flag for consecutive ones until a zero appears.
Technique and why it applies: The final bit is guaranteed zero. The number of consecutive ones immediately before it determines whether those ones form pairs with that final zero; parity indicates whether the final zero begins a one-bit character.
Invariant: ret tracks the parity of the run of ones immediately preceding the final zero.
Edge cases: A single-bit input [0] returns True because the reversed slice is empty. The problem guarantees the final bit is zero.
Complexity: The scan takes O(n) time and O(1) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether the last character in the bit sequence is encoded as a one-bit character.
Idea: Count the parity of consecutive ones immediately before the guaranteed final zero.
Technique and why it applies: The scan walks backward from the second-last bit, toggling parity for each one and stopping at the first zero. An even run means the last zero begins a one-bit character; an odd run means it is part of a two-bit character.
Invariant: parity is the parity of the suffix of ones immediately before the last bit.
Edge cases: A one-element [0] array returns True because the loop is empty. The problem guarantees bits ends with zero.
Complexity: The backward scan is O(n) time and O(1) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest common contiguous subarray of nums1 and nums2.
Idea: Use DP where matching elements extend a diagonal run and mismatches reset the state to zero.
Technique and why it applies: A common subarray must be contiguous, so equal values at positions row and col extend the match ending at the previous pair of positions. The maximum length is updated on each match.
Invariant: dp[row][col] is intended to store the common suffix length ending at nums2[row] and nums1[col].
Edge cases: The code allocates extra row/column but indexes dp[row][col] instead of dp[row+1][col+1]; at row or col zero, negative indices wrap to the final row/column, causing incorrect results. The indexing needs correction.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(mn) time and the table uses O(mn) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the kth smallest absolute difference among all unordered pairs of numbers.
Idea: Enumerate every pair, maintain a max-heap of the k smallest distances seen, and return the largest distance in that heap.
Technique and why it applies: Distances are negated so the heap top represents the largest retained distance. Whenever more than k pairs are stored, the largest is removed, leaving the k smallest candidates.
Invariant: The heap contains the k smallest pair distances seen so far, with its root equal to the largest among them.
Edge cases: The code assumes k is valid and there are at least k pairs. nums[idx+1:] creates a slice for each outer iteration, adding extra copying.
Complexity: There are O(n²) pairs and each heap operation costs O(log k), giving O(n² log k) time and O(k) heap space, plus temporary slices. No labels were supplied.
